newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal's Socialists hit political turbulence.
newsitem.headline: Portugal's Socialists hit political turbulence.

text.p: Half-way through their four-year term, Portugal's ruling Socialists are looking jaded as problems from striking pilots to internal dissent take their toll, political analysts said on Monday.

Back from a week-long trip to Latin America, Prime Minister Antonio Guterres faced some delicate domestic diplomacy to end a row between the Socialist "old guard" and the parliamentary leadership, the latest in a series of public spats that have shaken party unity.

Pilots at loss-making TAP-Air Portugal may have suspended a partial strike to give time for more talks, but rumbling troubles at the state airline are increasingly seen as a sign of government reluctance to tackle difficult political decisions head on, commentators say.
"The country is waiting for the prime minister...to try to bring a bit of order to the government," the Diario de Noticias wrote in a forthright editorial on Monday.
Not that the government record after two years in power is all negative. Far from it.

Portugal is now widely regarded, even by foreign economic analysts, as a near certainty for the European Union's single currency when the ambitious plan to wed the bloc's economies in monetary union is launched in 1999.

Finance Minister Antonio Sousa Franco, the politically independent former of head of the state court of accounts, has succeeded in pushing two deficit-cutting budgets through parliament, where the Socialists are four seats short of an absolute majority.
But even the austere Sousa Franco, who was drafted into the government when it took office in October 1995 to boost its economic credibility, has stumbled recently.
The quick-tempered minister, who makes no secret of his dislike of the political fray, was recently forced into an about-turn on value added tax (VAT) for small businesses and the self-employed.
After sending out the forms, the finance ministry cancelled them, apparently because of some administrative muddle.
Political opponents, however, said that the order had been rescinded because payment would have been due just before local authority elections in December.

Guterres was expected to meet party veteran Manuel Alegre later on Monday in an attempt to end the latest round of party infighting, triggered this time by the Socialist deputy's breaking of the official line in a parliamentary vote.

The vote was on a minor issue. But with former president Mario Soares weighing in on the side of Alegre, and the party's leader in parliament, Francisco Assis, threatening to stand down, Guterres was going to need all his political guile to prevent an embarrassing resignation from one side or the other.

The government's problems have been reflected in an eroding of its position in the opinion polls, although not to the point where opposition parties might be tempted to seek to force early elections, analysts say.

On the contrary, the main opposition Social Democrats, still seeking to regroup after their 1995 electoral defeat, have already said that they will not let the government fall before 1999, when monetary union starts.

But the Socialists, who proudly saw themselves as precursors of the British Labour Party's spectacular return to power in Britain earlier this year, have certainly lost their aura of invincibility, commentators and diplomats say.
"They seem to have lost their way a bit," said one European diplomat.
